title: Third declension

objectives.can: Parse third-declension nouns and find the stem from the genitive.

explanation.summary: The third declension is the largest and the least tidy of the five. Its nominative singular can end in almost anything, so the genitive singular, which always ends in -is, is the form that shows the stem. Learn nouns of this family as a pair, nominative and genitive.

sections.heading: Why the genitive matters
body: In the first and second declensions the nominative gives you the stem: *terra*, terr-; *filius*, fili-. In the third it often does not. *rex* has the stem reg-, as its genitive *regis* shows. *homo* has the stem homin-, from *hominis*. *nomen* has nomin-, from *nominis*. *pater* has patr-, from *patris*. The nominative has worn down; every other form is built on the stem that the genitive shows.
So a dictionary gives two forms: *rex, regis*. To decline the noun, take the genitive, remove -is, and add the endings. Always do this from the genitive, never from the nominative.

sections.heading: The endings
body: The third declension has masculine, feminine and neuter nouns, and the same endings serve for masculine and feminine. The neuter differs only in the nominative and accusative, which are alike, with -a in the plural.

Some endings overlap with the earlier declensions, especially -is (genitive singular here, dative and ablative plural in the first and second) and -e or -i in the ablative singular. The context and the noun's stem settle it. Where the tables below show a dash, the form usually exists but the analysis leaves it undecided: the dative plural of *homo* is homin-ibus, the same as the ablative, and the nominative plural of *nomen* is nomin-a.

sections.heading: Consonant stems and i-stems
body: Nouns whose stem ends in a consonant, like *rex*, *pater*, *homo*, *lex*, *virtus*, take the endings exactly as in the table: reg-um, not reg-ium. A group of nouns, the i-stems, keep an i before some endings. The commonest signs are a genitive plural in -ium, as in *montium* (from *mons*), *partium* (from *pars*) and *gentium* (from *gens*), and, for neuters, an ablative in -i. Many nouns in -is and -es, and many whose stem ends in two consonants (*mons*, *pars*, *gens*, *mors*), are i-stems. The nouns in -tas, like *civitas* and *veritas*, are consonant stems and take -um in the genitive plural: *civitatum*. The line between the two kinds is not firm, and some words waver; the texts themselves are not always consistent. You will recognise these by meeting them.
The point for reading is small: the third-declension genitive plural is -um or -ium, and you can safely read either as the genitive plural.

sections.heading: Three kinds of neuter
body: Neuter nouns of the third declension fall into a few patterns. Those in -men have the genitive in -minis: *nomen*, nominis. Those in -us, a large group, change the -s of the stem to -r between vowels: *corpus*, corporis; *tempus*, temporis; and *opus*, operis, which has -er- rather than -or-. A few, like *caput*, capitis, are irregular.
Because the neuter nominative and accusative are the same, you cannot tell subject from object by the ending. In the plural both end in -a: *tempora*, *nomina*.

sections.heading: Gender
body: The ending does not give the gender of a third-declension noun, and there are only rough guides. Nouns in -tas, in -x and the abstract nouns in -tus are mostly feminine: *civitas*, *veritas*, *virtus*, *pax*, *lex*, *vox*. Nouns in -or and most in -o are masculine, and *homo* and *rex* are masculine because they name men. Those in -men and in -us with a genitive in -oris or -eris are neuter. These are rough guides with exceptions, so learn the gender along with each word. An adjective that agrees with the noun will also show it.

misunderstandings: The nominative singular is not the stem. Do not make the accusative by adding -em to the nominative. The stems are reg- and homin-, and the accusatives are *regem* and *hominem*.

The ending -es is not one case. In the third declension it is nominative, accusative and vocative plural alike, as in *homines* and *fratres*; the analysis often leaves it undecided for that reason. The verb and the rest of the sentence show which it is.

The ending -is is not always genitive singular. In the third declension it is genitive singular (*hominis*), but in the first and second declensions -is is dative and ablative plural (*terris*). The genitive of the noun tells you which declension you are in.

A noun in -us is not always masculine. In the third declension *corpus* and *tempus* are neuter and *virtus* is feminine; the genitive (corporis, temporis, virtutis) shows that they are not second-declension words.

deeper.heading: Why there are so many patterns
body: The third declension merged two older classes, consonant stems and i-stems, whose endings had been different. Over time their endings crossed over, and in later Latin the distinction blurred further. This is why textbooks list exceptions and why the genitive plural of some words wavers between -um and -ium.
